strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing practical preference elicitation through natural language feedback
Sensible hybrid architecture that combines LLM strengths for language understanding with BO's principled uncertainty quantification and exploration
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 8+ environments with systematic ablation studies examining design choices (pairwise vs scalar, pair selection, prior knowledge)
Consistent empirical improvements over baselines in feedback-limited regimes across diverse utility function types
Excellent reproducibility support with detailed pseudocode, complete prompts, and implementation details in appendices
Practical design considerations demonstrated, including domain prior incorporation that significantly improves performance
weaknesses: Critical circular reasoning: human feedback is simulated by an LLM containing ground-truth utility functions in prompts (Appendix B.3), making it unclear whether results transfer to real human preferences. This oracle-informed setup fundamentally undermines the main claims

Lack of real-world validation: paper mentions 'real-world optimization campaigns in online A/B testing' but provides zero details, results, or evidence. All experiments use LLM-simulated oracle-informed feedback

Limited technical novelty: individual components (BO, preference learning, LLM few-shot learning) are well-established. Prior work exists on LLM + BO combinations (Liu et al. 2024, Austin et al. 2024). Contribution is primarily engineering-focused

Fading advantage in longer horizons: Figure 3 shows LILO's benefits diminish significantly by iteration 8, with baselines largely catching up, suggesting the natural language advantage applies only to early feedback-limited phases

Insufficient LLM reliability analysis: while using 5 samples per comparison, no investigation of consistency rates, failure modes, or systematic biases. Acknowledged fidelity limitations not deeply explored
Missing scalability analysis: no computational cost analysis despite requiring multiple LLM calls per pair per iteration. Practical deployment concerns unaddressed
No theoretical foundation: lacks convergence guarantees, sample complexity analysis, or theoretical characterization of when the hybrid approach is beneficial
Design choice justification limited: multiple decisions (K=64 pairs, 5 LLM samples, specific prompts) appear somewhat arbitrary with insufficient principled justification

Assumption of preference consistency unrealistic: framework assumes consistent utility function but real humans exhibit preference reversals and context-dependent preferences; no robustness analysis provided
Cold-start initialization: DM's first message hard-coded in experiments, making true cold-start performance assessment impossible and reducing practical applicability

Experimental limitations: quantitative baselines receive ground-truth feedback while LILO receives LLM-simulated feedback (asymmetric setup), only 4 outcome functions tested, no formal statistical significance tests, no human user studies

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing practical need for natural language preferences in optimization
Sensible system design placing LLM in supporting role to translate feedback while preserving BO's principled uncertainty quantification and acquisition functions

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple synthetic and real-world problems with thorough ablations on key design choices (pairwise vs scalar, pair selection, batch sizes, LLM models, prior knowledge)
Excellent reproducibility with extensive pseudo-code, all prompts, and simulation details in appendices
Consistent empirical improvements over baselines especially in feedback-limited regimes
weaknesses: Critical methodological flaw: entire evaluation relies on LLM-simulated human feedback where simulator has ground-truth utilities in prompt (Appendix B.3). This contradicts the core premise that natural language feedback captures genuine human preferences. No real human studies validate the approach works with actual decision makers

Unclear source of improvements: cannot distinguish whether gains come from natural language interface, question generation, LLM domain knowledge, or simply having more total feedback (pairs + conversation) than baselines. Evidence suggests pre-trained LLM knowledge and additional feedback matter substantially

Unfair baseline comparisons: True Utility BO receives oracle access to ground-truth utilities; Preferential BO receives fewer total feedback turns (only Bpf pairs vs LILO's pairs plus conversational turns). Confounds information amount with interface quality

Limited technical novelty: core method is straightforward application of existing techniques (pairwise preference learning + standard BO). Main contribution is problem formulation rather than novel algorithms or theoretical insights

Short optimization horizons (only T=8 iterations, ~16 total feedback queries) with unclear persistence of benefits over longer practical horizons typical in BO applications (hundreds-thousands evaluations)

Robustness to LLM failures under-explored: method assumes LLM consistency, but Section 4.3.1 shows scalar predictions are less reliable than pairwise comparisons, suggesting consistency issues not thoroughly investigated. No analysis of failure modes, contradiction handling, or out-of-distribution behavior

Ad-hoc prior knowledge incorporation: Section 4.3.3 shows domain/point/area priors give substantial gains (often larger than improvement to baselines), suggesting method relies more on LLM pre-trained knowledge than learning from feedback. Priors require privileged information about true function quantiles

Missing comparisons with preference elicitation literature: no comparison with decades of principled research on preference elicitation, making it unclear if LILO's question generation is superior or simply plausible
Artificial ground-truth utility functions, especially for Thermal Comfort which uses ISO standards rather than real human preferences; using these as evaluation ground truth is somewhat circular

Insufficient analysis of when natural language helps: ablation shows pairwise LLM comparisons only modestly outperform scalar predictions (Figure 4a), questioning the claimed advantage of language richness, and semantic outcomes substantially outperform synthetic DTLZ2

strengths: Well-motivated hybrid approach that leverages complementary strengths of LLMs (language understanding, domain knowledge) and BO (principled uncertainty, calibrated acquisition functions)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 8+ test problems with 30 replications each, systematic ablations on key design choices, proper baselines including oracle methods
Thorough methodological exposition with complete algorithmic details, prompts, and implementation specifics enabling reproducibility
Demonstrates consistent empirical improvements over relevant baselines, particularly in early optimization phases where sample efficiency matters most
Practical design insights validated through ablations: pairwise comparisons > scalar utilities, natural language feedback effectiveness, prior knowledge integration
Clear presentation with effective use of example conversations showing realistic interaction patterns with decision makers
weaknesses: Critical limitation: No validation with actual human feedback. Entire evaluation uses LLM-simulated human preferences without verifying whether simulated feedback reflects real human decision-making or information content. This is fundamental to claims about practical applicability.

Comparison fairness issue: LILO receives richer feedback (outcome history, natural language context, LLM domain knowledge extraction) while baselines receive only selected point feedback, making it difficult to isolate the contribution of natural language interpretation vs. additional information access

Diminishing advantages over optimization iterations: LILO's edge over true/preferential BO is largest early but erodes substantially by iteration 8, with baselines nearly converging in some environments. Questions remain about whether early gains reflect richer initial information rather than better exploitation.

Insufficient reliability quantification for LLM pairwise labeling: Paper uses 5 LLM samples per prediction but doesn't report agreement rates, consistency metrics, or how often ensemble predictions diverge. This is critical for understanding noise in utility estimates.

Lack of theoretical grounding: No convergence analysis, sample complexity bounds, or error propagation study. How do LLM calibration errors and pairwise mislabeling affect BO guarantees? Under what conditions are LLM-derived utility estimates reliable?
Computational cost opacity: Multiple LLM calls per iteration (5 samples × K pairs = ~320 calls/iteration) not analyzed. For practical deployment, total cost vs. baselines is crucial but missing.

Weak real-world evidence: Abstract and discussion claim deployment in 'real-world A/B testing campaigns' with zero substantiation—no metrics, details, or validation provided. Significantly undermines practical claims.
Limited analysis of failure modes and robustness: No discussion of when approach struggles, how it handles LLM misinterpretations, or behavior with non-monotonic/adversarial feedback.

strengths: Well-motivated practical problem combining natural language feedback with Bayesian optimization through a principled hybrid approach that preserves BO's calibrated uncertainty
Demonstrates natural language feedback is information-dense (~8-16 pairwise comparisons per NL statement), with comprehensive experiments across 10 diverse environments

Comprehensive experimental validation with proper baselines (LLM-only methods, quantitative feedback methods), 32 replications, and extensive ablations covering feedback batch size, prior knowledge, acquisition functions, and LLM choice
Technically sound integration of LLM preference interpretation with pairwise GP modeling and qEUBO acquisition; validates pairwise labeling outperforms direct utility scoring
Extensible to high-dimensional unstructured outcomes (text summarization) without explicit outcome space modeling; includes textual prior knowledge incorporation for warm-starting
Excellent reproducibility with all prompts provided, detailed algorithms, implementation details, and promised code release; clear writing with effective problem formulation
weaknesses: Critical limitation: all experiments use LLM-simulated decision makers, not real humans; unclear how LILO handles real human feedback inconsistency, cognitive biases, and non-transitivity—severely limits practical applicability claims

LILO's advantage diminishes substantially over longer horizons (Figure 14), with quantitative baselines matching/exceeding LILO by trial 16; main experiments (T=8) are in the regime where LILO excels but may not reflect realistic budget-limited settings

Limited theoretical analysis: no convergence guarantees, regret bounds, or formal treatment of how LLM label noise (85-90% accuracy from Figure 13) propagates through optimization; unclear whether pairwise GP adequately handles this noise

Heavy dependence on LLM quality and consistency not thoroughly investigated: same LLM used for both LILO and simulated DM introduces correlation; only 3 LLM variants tested; no analysis of robustness to systematic LLM biases
Posterior calibration unclear under label noise: with 85-90% LLM accuracy, uncertainty estimates may not reflect true model uncertainty; no validation that GP posterior remains meaningful/calibrated

Incomplete practical guidance: LLM API costs not discussed; labeling budget K and chunk size S sensitivity not explored; scalability in high-dimensional parameter/outcome spaces unclear; initialization sensitivity (Figure 12) shows strong dependence on prior quality but limited analysis

strengths: Well-motivated problem combining preference-based BO with natural language feedback
Sensible hybrid architecture leveraging LLMs for preference extraction while preserving principled BO acquisition
Comprehensive experimental methodology with 10 test problems, multiple baselines, extensive ablations, and 32 replications
Clear demonstration that natural language can convey information equivalent to 8-16 pairwise comparisons (Figure 4)
Thorough implementation details and promised code release enabling reproducibility
weaknesses: Critical limitation: All experiments use LLM-simulated feedback where the DM simulator has access to ground-truth utility—unrealistic and unvalidated on real human feedback; no human studies despite claiming to enable preference elicitation

Confounded experimental setup: LILO receives rich natural language feedback while quantitative baselines receive only binary comparisons; improvements are modest (1-3%) and often diminish significantly in longer horizons (Appendix F.5)
Limited novelty: Combines established components (pairwise GP from Chu & Ghahramani 2005, EUBO from Lin et al. 2022, standard LLM prompting) without new theoretical insights or algorithmic advances
Heavy dependence on prompt engineering (6+ domain-specific prompts in Appendix B.2) with no systematic sensitivity analysis or guidance for practitioners on adapting to new domains

No theoretical analysis: Missing convergence guarantees, sample complexity bounds, characterization of when LILO should be preferred, or analysis of how label errors propagate through the optimization loop

Practical applicability unclear: Missing cost model (LLM API calls), no comparison to human feedback costs, scalability concerns with quadratic pair explosion, and advantages concentrated in short horizons (8 trials)

Overclaiming and incomplete positioning: 'Consistently outperforms' statements overstated; improvements often marginal; limited engagement with active preference learning and learning-to-rank literature; no discussion of contradictory feedback or feedback inconsistency handling

strengths: Novel integration of free-form natural language feedback with principled Bayesian optimization, providing an expressive interface beyond pairwise comparisons while maintaining calibrated uncertainty and acquisition-driven exploration

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 10 diverse benchmarks with multiple utility function types, proper statistical analysis (32 replications, 95% CIs), extensive ablations, and extension to unstructured outcomes (text summarization)
Strong empirical demonstration that a single natural language message can outperform 8-16 pairwise comparisons, establishing the information density of natural language feedback
Excellent reproducibility: complete algorithms, all 12 prompts, detailed baseline implementations, exact utility specifications, and promised code release—a model example of transparency standards
Honest and thorough treatment of limitations including simulated feedback, LLM dependency, horizon effects, and realistic discussion of applicability scope and future directions
weaknesses: Experiments use simulated rather than real human feedback, with the simulated DM provided ground-truth utilities—a significant limitation that undermines claims about practical applicability despite enabling controlled evaluation
Limited theoretical grounding: no convergence guarantees, sample complexity analysis, or formal treatment of LLM label uncertainty; depends on empirical noise modeling via probit likelihood

Narrow window of practical advantage: LILO's superiority concentrated in early iterations (Figure 3, 14); quantitative baselines catch up or surpass it after ~8 trials, limiting applicability to truly feedback-limited regimes

Strong LLM dependency with limited analysis: only large models tested in ablations (70B, 17B, 14B); smaller models fail due to JSON parsing; scalability and performance degradation with model quality underexplored

Fairness and comparison concerns: information-density comparison assumes effort equivalence between one NL message and 8-16 comparisons without empirical justification of cognitive load; quantitative baselines use noiseless oracle feedback; LLM(2-step) is an internal ablation rather than independent baseline
